title: IPMAT Indore VA Full Sectional Mock - Set 09 (Advanced Level)

questions.passage:
In 1975, the economist Charles Goodhart, advising the Bank of England, observed that any statistical regularity tends to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes. The anthropologist Marilyn Strathern later compressed this into the aphorism that now bears his name: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. The remark is usually received as a warning about perverse incentives: the hospital that shortens its waiting list by reclassifying patients, the school that lifts its pass rate by discouraging weak students from sitting the examination. But to read Goodhart's law merely as a catalogue of cheating is to miss its deeper and more unsettling implication, which is that measurement is not a neutral act of observation but an intervention that reorganises the thing observed.

Consider the origins of the modern statistic. In the early nineteenth century, European states began to gather numbers about their populations, such as births, deaths, crimes and suicides, with the ambition of rendering society legible. James C. Scott has argued that such legibility was never innocent: a state that cannot see its citizens cannot tax, conscript or reform them, and so the census, the cadastral map and the standardised surname were instruments of simplification, flattening local variation into categories that administrators could handle. Yet the early statisticians themselves believed they were discovering laws, much as astronomers had discovered the laws of planetary motion. Adolphe Quetelet's "average man" was offered not as a convenient fiction but as a social ideal around which the deviations of real individuals clustered like errors around a true value. The very word "statistics" betrays this origin; it is the science of the state.

What the pioneers underestimated was reflexivity. Planets do not read astronomy; people read statistics. The philosopher Ian Hacking called this the "looping effect" of human kinds: when a classification is introduced, whether the "teenager", the "multiple personality" or the "obese", those classified alter their behaviour in response, which in turn revises the classification. A category of persons is thus not a fixed natural kind but a moving target, partly authored by the act of naming. The social sciences, accordingly, can never quite catch up with their own subject; every finding is a message to the very people it describes, who may heed it, resist it or exploit it. Economists know a version of this as the Lucas critique: a model calibrated on past behaviour fails when policy changes, because agents change how they behave once the rules change.

The most famous illustration of the underlying problem is probably apocryphal. A Soviet nail factory, the story goes, was assessed by the weight of its output and so produced a handful of enormous, useless spikes; when the plan was revised to reward the number of nails, it turned out thousands of tiny ones, each too small to hold anything. Whether or not any factory behaved so, the story endures because it dramatises a structural feature rather than a moral failing: the managers are not villains but rational agents responding precisely to the signal they were given. The pathology lies in the gap between what the planners wanted, which was usable nails, and what they could cheaply observe, which was tonnage or tally. Every metric is a proxy, and the more weight a proxy is made to bear, the stronger the incentive to optimise the proxy at the expense of the thing it stands for.

None of this has prevented the extraordinary spread of metrics into domains once governed by professional judgement. Universities are ranked, and so adjust their admissions to the ranking's formula; surgeons are scored on mortality, and so some quietly decline the hardest cases; police forces are assessed on recorded crime, and so some record burglaries as "suspicious incidents". Defenders of metrics reply, with some justice, that the alternative, trust in unaccountable expertise, has its own record of failure, from complacent clinicians to captured regulators. Numbers, after all, can be audited by outsiders, whereas intuition cannot. The choice, they insist, is not between metrics and wisdom but between visible error and invisible error. The reply is not trivial. But it conceals a sleight of hand: it assumes that the visibility of a metric's error is equivalent to its correctability, when in fact a gamed metric often fails silently, its apparent precision lending false assurance precisely when it has decoupled from reality.

A more constructive response comes from a surprising direction. Engineers designing safety systems have long recognised that no single indicator can be trusted once operators know it is being watched; their remedy is redundancy, in which several imperfectly correlated measures are monitored together, so that manipulating one tends to betray itself in the others. The principle generalises. A school judged by examination results, attendance and the later earnings of its graduates is harder to game than one judged by any of these alone, not because the three are individually sound but because the cheapest ways of improving one tend to damage another. Such a portfolio of metrics does not restore innocence to measurement; it merely raises the cost of deception. Still, it suggests that the lesson of Goodhart is not that numbers should be abandoned but that they should be held loosely: treated as evidence to be interpreted by someone accountable for the interpretation, rather than as verdicts that dispense with it.

There is a final irony. The movement to quantify public life was animated by a distrust of discretion, yet every metric requires discretion at its birth: someone must decide what counts as a crime, a graduate, a completed treatment. These decisions are made once, early, and then forgotten, hardening into the apparently objective facts on which later arguments rest. Few people, afterwards, think to revisit them. To audit a number properly is therefore to recover the judgement buried within it. The numbers do not replace the human decision; they bury it, and a society that forgets where its judgements were buried will find them again only when something breaks.
questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?
options: A) Goodhart's law reveals widespread cheating in public institutions, which can be curbed only by replacing numerical targets with professional discretion.
B) Measuring social life changes what is measured, so numbers are best treated as evidence needing accountable interpretation.
C) Social categories are partly created by the act of classification, which is why the social sciences cannot be genuinely scientific.
D) The spread of state statistics was driven chiefly by a wish to control populations, which explains why modern metrics are manipulated.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage opens by rejecting the 'catalogue of cheating' reading (so A is out) and moves to the claim that measurement is an intervention. It ends by recommending metrics 'held loosely' as evidence under accountable interpretation. C and D take single supporting strands (Hacking, Scott) as the whole thesis; C also wrongly concludes social science is unscientific, which the author never says.

questions.question: The author remarks that "planets do not read astronomy; people read statistics" primarily in order to
options: A) suggest that early statisticians were less rigorous than the astronomers whose methods they sought to imitate in studying society.
B) argue that human behaviour, unlike planetary motion, is too unpredictable to be captured by any mathematical model at all.
C) show that social science should abandon laws for interpretive methods.
D) mark a difference between natural and social subject matter that the early statisticians failed to take into account.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The sentence follows 'What the pioneers underestimated was reflexivity'. Its job is to contrast a passive natural subject with a social subject that reacts to findings. A criticises rigour (not the issue); B overstates ('any model at all'); C prescribes a remedy the author never offers.

questions.question: The "sleight of hand" that the author attributes to the defenders of metrics (paragraph 5) lies in
options: A) treating an error that can be seen as though it were an error that will be corrected.
B) pretending that expert judgement has never been wrong.
C) presenting audits as an adequate replacement for the metrics themselves.
D) assuming that the failures of professional experts show that metrics can never be captured by interested parties.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The author states it directly: defenders assume 'visibility of a metric's error is equivalent to its correctability'. B contradicts the passage, since defenders concede expertise has 'its own record of failure'. C and D are not claims the passage attributes to them.

questions.question: Each of the following is mentioned in the passage as a response to being measured EXCEPT
options: A) Schools discouraging weaker pupils from sitting examinations
B) Surgeons declining to operate on the most difficult cases
C) Universities cutting tuition fees to climb the rankings
D) Police forces recording burglaries as 'suspicious incidents'
questions.explanation: Explanation: A is in paragraph 1, B and D in paragraph 5. Universities are said to 'adjust their admissions' to the ranking formula; fee-cutting is never mentioned.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's case for monitoring a portfolio of metrics (paragraph 6)?
options: A) Operators in safety-critical industries are found to monitor fewer indicators than the administrators of schools do.
B) Selecting high-achieving pupils lifts results, attendance and graduates' earnings together.
C) Maintaining several indicators is considerably more costly for institutions than maintaining a single one.
D) Some schools have been found to inflate attendance records without any corresponding rise in examination results.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The case rests on the cheapest ways of improving one measure damaging another, so gaming betrays itself. If one cheap tactic (selective admission) inflates all three at once, gaming no longer shows up as inconsistency. C concerns cost to institutions, not gameability. D actually supports the author: the attendance manipulation is exposed by flat results.

None of this has prevented the extraordinary spread of metrics into domains once governed by professional judgement. Universities are ranked, and so adjust their admissions to the ranking's formula; surgeons are scored on mortality, and so some quietly decline the hardest cases; police forces are assessed on recorded crime, and so some record burglaries as "suspicious incidents". Defenders of metrics reply, with some justice, that the alternative, trust in unaccountable expertise, has its own record of failure, from complacent clinicians to captured regulators. Numbers, after all, can be audited by outsiders, whereas intuition cannot. The choice, they insist, is not between metrics and wisdom but between visible error and invisible error. The reply is not trivial. But it conceals a sleight of hand: it assumes that the visibility of a metric's error is equivalent to its correctability, when in fact a gamed metric often fails silently, its apparent precision lending false assurance precisely when it has decoupled from reality.

A more constructive response comes from a surprising direction. Engineers designing safety systems have long recognised that no single indicator can be trusted once operators know it is being watched; their remedy is redundancy, in which several imperfectly correlated measures are monitored together, so that manipulating one tends to betray itself in the others. The principle generalises. A school judged by examination results, attendance and the later earnings of its graduates is harder to game than one judged by any of these alone, not because the three are individually sound but because the cheapest ways of improving one tend to damage another. Such a portfolio of metrics does not restore innocence to measurement; it merely raises the cost of deception. Still, it suggests that the lesson of Goodhart is not that numbers should be abandoned but that they should be held loosely: treated as evidence to be interpreted by someone accountable for the interpretation, rather than as verdicts that dispense with it.

There is a final irony. The movement to quantify public life was animated by a distrust of discretion, yet every metric requires discretion at its birth: someone must decide what counts as a crime, a graduate, a completed treatment. These decisions are made once, early, and then forgotten, hardening into the apparently objective facts on which later arguments rest. Few people, afterwards, think to revisit them. To audit a number properly is therefore to recover the judgement buried within it. The numbers do not replace the human decision; they bury it, and a society that forgets where its judgements were buried will find them again only when something breaks.
questions.question: Which of the following is the best example of the "looping effect" described in paragraph 3?
options: A) A government publishes unemployment figures, which are later revised upward once more complete data arrive from employers.
B) A school ranks pupils by grade, and some pupils begin cheating in order to improve their positions in the ranking.
C) A diagnostic label gains currency, people come to understand themselves through it, and the criteria are then revised.
D) A central bank predicts a recession, cuts rates in response, and thereby prevents the recession it had predicted.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Hacking's loop needs a classification of kinds of people, those classified changing in response, and the classification being revised in turn. Only C has all three. B is Goodhart's law (target and gaming), not a loop in a human kind; D is a self-defeating forecast about the economy, not a category of persons.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence:

The minister's promise to "revisit" the policy was, in effect, a ________ offered to quieten critics rather than a genuine change of course.
options: A) sop
B) gambit
C) catharsis
D) mandate
questions.explanation: Explanation: A 'sop' is something given to appease. A 'gambit' is an opening move made to gain advantage, usually involving some risk or sacrifice, which does not fit a promise that costs the government nothing. 'Catharsis' and 'mandate' do not fit the sense.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence:

Having built a reputation for scrupulous neutrality over three decades, the editor found it ________ by a single injudicious remark on live television.
options: A) mitigated
B) expiated
C) palliated
D) vitiated
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Vitiated' means spoiled or impaired. 'Mitigated' and 'palliated' mean lessened or eased; 'expiated' means atoned for. Only 'vitiated' conveys damage to the reputation.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence:

The new regulations were criticised as a mere fig leaf, since they ________.
options: A) banned the practice outright and imposed severe penalties on every violator
B) left the underlying conduct essentially untouched while appearing to address it
C) were drafted in consultation with the very industry they claimed to regulate, and were passed unanimously
D) extended to all firms regardless of their size
questions.explanation: Explanation: A fig leaf covers something without removing it. Only B describes the appearance of action with no substantive change. A describes strong action; D is neutral. C is tempting, but it describes how the rules were made, not that they were ineffective.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best fills the blanks:

Far from being ________ in the face of criticism, the author grew more ________, doubling down on claims that even her allies found ________.
options: A) undaunted; truculent; unassailable
B) contrite; amenable; indefensible
C) chastened; obdurate; untenable
D) complacent; diffident; irrefutable
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Far from being chastened' (made subdued) she 'doubled down', so she grew obdurate (stubborn), and allies found the claims untenable (impossible to defend). In A, 'far from being undaunted' contradicts the doubling down; C's 'amenable' (agreeable) and D's 'diffident' contradict it too.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best fills the blanks:

The government's ________ response to the crisis, a ________ of half-measures announced with great fanfare, did little to ________ public anxiety.
options: A) fulsome; litany; exacerbate
B) perfunctory; farrago; stoke
C) draconian; panoply; inflame
D) tepid; patchwork; allay
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Half-measures' with little effect call for 'tepid' and 'patchwork', and a response that fails to 'allay' (relieve) anxiety. B fits the first two blanks, but 'did little to stoke anxiety' makes no sense; 'draconian' contradicts half-measures.

questions.question:
Choose the best replacement for the portion in square brackets:

Each of the proposals, along with its appendices, [have been scrutinised closely by] the review board before the final list was announced.
options: A) has been scrutinised closely by
B) were scrutinised closely by
C) has scrutinised closely
D) have been closely scrutinised from
questions.explanation: Explanation: The subject is 'Each', which is singular. 'Along with its appendices' is parenthetical and does not make the subject plural. So the verb must be 'has been', and the passive 'by the review board' must be kept.

questions.question:
Choose the best replacement for the portion in square brackets:

Having been warned repeatedly about the risks, [the project was pursued by the board] regardless of the cost.
options: A) the pursuit of the project was undertaken by the board
B) the project was still pursued by the board
C) the board pursued the project
D) pursuing the project was the board's decision
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Having been warned' needs the warned party, the board, as its grammatical subject. In A, B and D the subject is 'pursuit', 'project' or 'pursuing', so the modifier dangles.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'Historians have long blamed a single catastrophic fire for the disappearance of the great library of Alexandria. Yet the evidence points to something far less dramatic. ________ Funding dwindled as successive rulers lost interest in scholarship, scholars drifted away to patrons elsewhere, and the scrolls, written on papyrus that crumbles without constant recopying, simply decayed. What vanished was not a building consumed in a night but an institution starved over centuries.'
options: A) The collection dwindled over centuries through neglect, with no single act of destruction to blame.
B) The fire did occur, and later chroniclers, eager for a dramatic story, simply exaggerated how much of the collection it consumed.
C) Few writers of the period mention the library, which has led some scholars to doubt that it ever existed in any real sense.
D) The scrolls were removed to Rome, where they were lost in later wars.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The blank must state the thesis that the sentences after it support: slow decline from neglect. B concedes a fire, against 'far less dramatic'; C questions the library's existence, but the passage speaks of its 'disappearance'; D introduces Rome, unsupported by what follows.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'Economists often treat price as a neutral signal of scarcity. But in markets for trust goods such as legal advice, medical care and education, price also functions as a signal of quality, because buyers cannot judge the product for themselves. ________ A lawyer who halves her fees may find clients fleeing rather than flocking, since the discount is read as a confession of inferiority. The ordinary logic of competition, in which the cheaper seller wins, is thereby inverted.'
options: A) Regulators have consequently sought to cap the fees that professionals in these fields may charge their clients.
B) Sellers of such services therefore compete chiefly on convenience, since buyers value their time more than their money.
C) In such markets, a higher price will always attract more customers, whatever the quality actually delivered.
D) In such markets, a lower price can therefore deter customers instead of attracting them.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The next sentences give a lowered price repelling clients, and the last sentence speaks of inverted competition. D is the general claim they illustrate. C overgeneralises ('always', 'whatever the quality') and is about higher prices, which the passage never tests.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: A) The arbitrator, being wholly disinterested in the outcome of the dispute, was trusted by both parties to rule fairly.
B) Several firms continue to flaunt the new emission norms, confident that penalties will rarely be imposed.
C) Her speech was designed to elicit sympathy from the audience rather than to inform them of the facts.
D) The auditors were careful to ensure that no discrepancy, however small, escaped their notice during the review.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Flaunt' means to display ostentatiously; to openly disregard a rule is to 'flout' it. 'Disinterested' (impartial), 'elicit' (draw out) and 'ensure' (make certain) are all used correctly.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: A) From the minister's silence, the reporters implied that the scandal ran deeper than admitted.
B) The board's assent to the merger came only after several weeks of tense and difficult negotiation.
C) The wine's acidity is a perfect complement to the richness of the dish it was served with.
D) The committee comprises twelve members who are drawn from six different regions of the country.
questions.explanation: Explanation: To 'imply' is to suggest something to others; the reporters drew a conclusion from the silence, so they 'inferred'. 'Assent', 'complement' and 'comprises' are all correct.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. This "framing effect" was hard to reconcile with a model in which only outcomes, and not their wording, should matter.
2. For most of the twentieth century, economists assumed that people choose among options by calculating their expected benefit.
3. Its acceptance forced the discipline to admit that rationality is better treated as an achievement of careful reflection than as a default setting.
4. Experiments by Kahneman and Tversky, however, showed that choices shift depending on how the same options are described.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 2 sets up the old assumption. 4 opens with 'however' to contradict it. 1 names the finding ('This framing effect') introduced in 4. 3 follows with 'Its acceptance', referring to the framing effect, and gives the consequence. Order: 2-4-1-3.

questions.passage:
Interviewer: Governor, critics say the bank moved too late. Is that fair?

Governor: It's fair to say we moved later than hindsight would advise, but hindsight is a luxury policymakers don't have. In 2021 the price increases looked concentrated in a few categories, such as used cars and shipping, and the textbook response to a supply shock is to look through it, because raising rates cannot unclog a port. What changed our minds was breadth: when the increases spread to services, where prices are sticky and driven by wages, it stopped looking like a supply shock and started looking like a demand problem.

Interviewer: So the mistake was one of classification, not of nerve?

Governor: I'd resist drawing that distinction too neatly. Classification is a judgement made under uncertainty, and nerve is what it takes to act on a judgement before the data confirm it. We had the first and, in the early months, not enough of the second.

Interviewer: Would you do anything differently?

Governor: I'd weigh the cost of being wrong asymmetrically. Acting early and being wrong costs a little growth; acting late and being wrong costs credibility, which takes years to rebuild.
questions.question: According to the Governor, the bank changed its assessment of inflation mainly because
options: A) shipping costs kept climbing for several quarters.
B) critics showed that raising rates could unclog ports.
C) wage growth slowed sharply once borrowing costs had begun to rise across the economy.
D) price increases broadened into services, where prices are sticky and wage-driven.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'What changed our minds was breadth': the spread of increases into wage-driven services. Shipping and used cars were the early, narrow signs; the Governor says rate rises 'cannot unclog a port', the opposite of B.

questions.question: The Governor's response to the "classification, not nerve" suggestion implies that he
options: A) denies that the bank made any error of judgement at all, given the data available at the time.
B) treats the two as connected, and admits to a shortfall in the second.
C) attributes the delay solely to the bank's wrongful classification of the price shock.
D) believes policymakers should never act on a judgement before the data confirm it.
questions.explanation: Explanation: He 'resists' the neat split, noting that nerve is needed to act on a classification, and says the bank had the first but not enough of the second. A and B ignore the admission; D is the opposite of his definition of nerve.
